justice: The street allocates substantial space to multiple users through wide vehicle lanes, side paths on both sides, and a planted median, indicating relatively balanced spatial distribution.

Both sides of the corridor appear to include separated edge spaces behind curbs and landscape strips, which supports fair access for pedestrians rather than dedicating the entire right-of-way to cars.

The sidewalks/side paths look continuous and generally level, but no curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked crossing points are visible in this frame, limiting confidence in full barrier-free accessibility.
Protective railings and planters along the median organize movement clearly, yet they may also reduce spontaneous mid-block access across the street for some users.
safety: Clear lane markings, a straight roadway, and low visible traffic volume support predictable vehicle movement and reduce immediate conflict risk.
A central median with fencing and planters separates opposing traffic streams, which improves crash protection for drivers and discourages unsafe crossings.
Streetlights are installed at regular intervals on both sides of the road, suggesting better nighttime visibility and surveillance.

Trees and side buffers create separation between the roadway and pedestrian realm, but no visible zebra crossing or signalized crossing is present in this view, which weakens pedestrian crossing safety.
livability: Street trees, landscaped edges, and planter boxes create a more pleasant everyday environment than a purely asphalt-dominated corridor.
Buildings along the left side appear to include active ground-floor commercial uses, which can support daily needs and street activity.
The corridor is wide, clean, and orderly, indicating a maintained urban environment that is likely comfortable for routine travel.
However, the road remains visually dominated by motor-vehicle space, so the social and public-life character is weaker than in a more pedestrian-oriented street.
sustainability: Continuous rows of trees and planted medians contribute to urban greening and help with shade, air-quality benefits, and heat mitigation.
The landscaped strips and planters suggest investment in green infrastructure rather than a fully sealed hardscape edge.
The broad side lanes/paths separated from main traffic may support lower-carbon modes, although dedicated bicycle symbols are not clearly visible.
No visible bus stop, transit shelter, or explicit stormwater features can be confirmed in the frame, so multimodal and water-sensitive sustainability evidence is only partial.
aesthetics: The boulevard has a strong visual order created by symmetrical streetlights, aligned trees, and consistent lane geometry.
Well-maintained planting beds, decorative planter boxes, and clean pavement contribute to a polished streetscape appearance.
The contrasting building forms on both sides are visually balanced by the green corridor, producing an attractive urban boulevard character.
The uncluttered roadway and limited roadside signage reduce visual chaos and strengthen overall coherence.
comfort: Rows of mature and semi-mature trees on both sides and in the median provide some shade potential, improving thermal comfort compared with a fully exposed roadway.
The pavement appears smooth and newly maintained, which supports physical comfort for drivers and likely for wheeled users on adjacent paths.
Generous separation between travel lanes and side areas reduces the sense of crowding and supports psychological comfort.
Even so, the roadway is very wide and exposed to sun in the center, and no benches or small-scale pedestrian amenities are visible, limiting comfort for people spending time outside vehicles.
walkability: Continuous side paths are visible on both sides of the street, indicating that pedestrians likely have a dedicated route separated from fast traffic.
Trees and landscape buffers improve the walking environment by adding enclosure and partial shade along the edges.
The long straight block and wide carriageway reduce crossing convenience, especially because no marked crosswalk is visible in this image.
The street reads more as a through-movement boulevard than a fine-grained pedestrian street, so walking is possible but not strongly prioritized.
bikeability: The corridor appears to include side lanes or frontage paths separated from main traffic, which may offer safer cycling space than mixing directly with fast vehicles.
Wide roadway design and clear lane discipline reduce erratic vehicle behavior, which can indirectly support cycling safety.
However, no clearly marked protected bike lane, bicycle symbol, or dedicated cycling signal is visible, so bicycle priority is uncertain.
The broad motor-traffic environment and long uninterrupted road geometry may feel intimidating for less confident cyclists despite the landscaped separation.
